stimuli.title: Document 3: The Federalist No. 51 (excerpts)
stimuli.html:
The Federalist Papers were 85 essays published in New York newspapers in 1787 and 1788 to urge voters to ratify the Constitution. They were signed with the pen name "Publius."

[1] But the great security against a gradual concentration of the several powers in the same department, consists in giving to those who administer each department the necessary constitutional means and personal motives to resist encroachments of the others. … Ambition must be made to counteract ambition. … If men were angels, no government would be necessary. If angels were to govern men, neither external nor internal controls on government would be necessary. In framing a government which is to be administered by men over men, the great difficulty lies in this: you must first enable the government to control the governed; and in the next place oblige it to control itself. A dependence on the people is, no doubt, the primary control on the government; but experience has taught mankind the necessity of auxiliary precautions.

[2] In the compound republic of America, the power surrendered by the people is first divided between two distinct governments, and then the portion allotted to each subdivided among distinct and separate departments. Hence a double security arises to the rights of the people.
stimuli.source: James Madison, The Federalist No. 51, published February 1788

stimuli.title: Document 4: The U.S. Constitution on National and State Power (excerpts)
stimuli.html:
Article I, Section 8 (selected powers of Congress). The Congress shall have Power … To borrow Money on the credit of the United States; To regulate Commerce with foreign Nations, and among the several States, and with the Indian Tribes; … To coin Money, regulate the Value thereof … To declare War … To make all Laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into Execution the foregoing Powers …

Article I, Section 10. No State shall enter into any Treaty, Alliance, or Confederation; … coin Money; emit Bills of Credit …

Article VI. This Constitution, and the Laws of the United States which shall be made in Pursuance thereof; and all Treaties made, or which shall be made, under the Authority of the United States, shall be the supreme Law of the Land; and the Judges in every State shall be bound thereby, any Thing in the Constitution or Laws of any State to the Contrary notwithstanding.

Tenth Amendment (1791). The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people.
stimuli.source: Constitution of the United States (1787) and Tenth Amendment (ratified 1791). "Bills of Credit" means paper money.

stimuli.title: Presidential Vetoes and Overrides, 1981–2025
stimuli.html: A president can veto (reject) a bill passed by Congress. Congress can override a regular veto if two-thirds of the House and two-thirds of the Senate vote to pass the bill again; the bill then becomes law without the president's signature. The graph shows the total number of vetoes issued by seven presidents and how many of those vetoes Congress overrode.
stimuli.source: U.S. Senate, "Summary of Bills Vetoed, 1789–present." Totals include regular and pocket vetoes.

stimuli.title: Document 6: The U.S. Constitution, Article I and Article II (excerpts)
stimuli.html:
Article I, Section 2. The House of Representatives shall be composed of Members chosen every second Year by the People of the several States …

Article I, Section 3. The Senate of the United States shall be composed of two Senators from each State, chosen by the Legislature thereof, for six Years; and each Senator shall have one Vote.

Article II, Section 2. The President shall be Commander in Chief of the Army and Navy of the United States … He shall have Power, by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate, to make Treaties, provided two thirds of the Senators present concur; and he shall nominate, and by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate, shall appoint Ambassadors, other public Ministers and Consuls, Judges of the supreme Court, and all other Officers of the United States …
stimuli.source: Constitution of the United States, signed September 17, 1787. The Seventeenth Amendment (1913) changed Article I, Section 3 so that senators are elected directly by the people of each state.

stimuli.title: Document 7: The U.S. Constitution on Impeachment (excerpts)
stimuli.html:
Article I, Section 2. The House of Representatives … shall have the sole Power of Impeachment.

Article I, Section 3. The Senate shall have the sole Power to try all Impeachments. … And no Person shall be convicted without the Concurrence of two thirds of the Members present.

Article II, Section 4. The President, Vice President and all civil Officers of the United States, shall be removed from Office on Impeachment for, and Conviction of, Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors.
stimuli.source: Constitution of the United States, signed September 17, 1787. "Concurrence" means agreement. "Civil Officers" include federal judges and cabinet members.

stimuli.title: Document 8: The Federalist Nos. 47 and 78 (excerpts)
stimuli.html:
The Federalist Papers were 85 essays published in New York newspapers in 1787 and 1788 to urge voters to ratify the Constitution.

[1] The accumulation of all powers, legislative, executive, and judiciary, in the same hands, whether of one, a few, or many, and whether hereditary, self-appointed, or elective, may justly be pronounced the very definition of tyranny. (James Madison, No. 47)

[2] The Executive not only dispenses the honors, but holds the sword of the community. The legislature not only commands the purse, but prescribes the rules by which the duties and rights of every citizen are to be regulated. The judiciary, on the contrary, has no influence over either the sword or the purse … It may truly be said to have neither FORCE nor WILL, but merely judgment; and must ultimately depend upon the aid of the executive arm even for the efficacy of its judgments. (Alexander Hamilton, No. 78)
stimuli.source: The Federalist Nos. 47 and 78, 1788. "Efficacy" means effectiveness.

stimuli.title: Document 9: The U.S. Constitution on National and State Power (excerpts)
stimuli.html:
Article I, Section 8 (selected powers of Congress). The Congress shall have Power To lay and collect Taxes, Duties, Imposts and Excises … To establish Post Offices and post Roads; … To raise and support Armies …

Article I, Section 10. No State shall, without the Consent of the Congress, lay any Imposts or Duties on Imports or Exports …

Article IV, Section 1. Full Faith and Credit shall be given in each State to the public Acts, Records, and judicial Proceedings of every other State.

Tenth Amendment (1791). The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people.
stimuli.source: Constitution of the United States (1787) and Tenth Amendment (ratified 1791). "Imposts" and "Duties" are taxes on goods, such as goods brought in from other countries.

stimuli.title: Amendments to the U.S. Constitution, 1789–2025
stimuli.html: Article V allows the Constitution to be amended. Congress proposes an amendment by a two-thirds vote of both houses, and three-fourths of the states must ratify it. The graph shows how many amendments were ratified in each period. As of 2025, 27 amendments have been ratified. The first ten, ratified together in 1791, are called the Bill of Rights.

items.prompt: According to Document 1, which part of the government is given the power to make laws?
options: Congress, made up of the Senate and the House of Representatives
The President of the United States, as the head of the executive
The Supreme Court, along with the lower courts Congress creates
The governments of the individual states, through their legislatures
why: The President holds the executive power (Article II), which is the power to enforce laws, not make them.
The courts hold the judicial power (Article III), which is the power to interpret laws, not make them.
Document 1 does not mention state governments at all. It describes the three branches of the national government.
items.hint: Making laws is called legislative power. Find the word "legislative."
items.explain:
Article I says, "All legislative Powers herein granted shall be vested in a Congress of the United States, which shall consist of a Senate and House of Representatives." Legislative power is the power to make laws, and vested in means "given to." So Congress makes the laws.

The President holds executive power (enforcing laws), and the courts hold judicial power (interpreting laws). Document 1 does not mention state governments at all.

items.prompt: Drag each power into the branch of the national government that holds it.
choices: Serve as commander in chief of the armed forces
Decide whether a law violates the Constitution
items.why: The most common mistake is placing "Declare war" with the President. The President commands the armed forces, but only Congress can declare war.
items.hint: Congress makes laws, the President enforces laws, and the courts interpret laws and decide cases.
items.explain:
• Legislative: Congress has the power to declare war (Article I, Section 8). The House impeaches officials and the Senate holds the trial and can remove them (Article I).
  • Executive: the President is commander in chief of the armed forces and can grant pardons for federal crimes (Article II, Section 2).
  • Judicial: courts decide whether laws violate the Constitution (judicial review) and hear cases, including cases between two states (Article III).

A common mix-up is placing "declare war" with the President. The President commands the military, but only Congress can declare war.

items.prompt: According to Document 2, what must the President do with a bill he does not approve?
options: Return it, with his objections, to the house of Congress where it started
Send it to the Supreme Court so the justices can rule on whether it is constitutional
Send it to the state legislatures, which hold a final vote on whether it becomes law
Hold it until voters can decide its fate in the next national election
why: Courts do not review bills before they become law. Document 2 says the President returns the bill to Congress.
Document 2 never mentions the states. The bill goes back to the house of Congress where it started.
Document 2 says nothing about elections. It says the President "shall return it, with his Objections."
items.hint: Find the words "but if not" and read what comes next.
items.explain:
The excerpt says, "If he approve he shall sign it, but if not he shall return it, with his Objections to that House in which it shall have originated." Originated means "started." This is the veto.

The Supreme Court does not review bills before they become law; it rules on laws in actual cases after they take effect. Document 2 says nothing about states or elections.

items.prompt: Both houses of Congress approve a proposed amendment by a two-thirds vote. Over the next three years, the legislatures of 36 of the 50 states vote to ratify it. What is the status of the amendment?
options: It is not yet part of the Constitution, because 38 states must ratify it
It is part of the Constitution, because 36 states is more than two-thirds of 50
It is not yet part of the Constitution, because the president must sign it first
It is part of the Constitution, because a majority of the states have ratified it
why: Two-thirds is the fraction Congress needs to propose. Ratifying needs three-fourths of the states: 50 × 3/4 = 37.5, so 38.
The president has no role in the amendment process under Article V. The problem is the number of states.
A majority is not enough. Article V requires three-fourths of the states, which is 38 of 50.
items.hint: Propose = two-thirds of Congress. Ratify = three-fourths of the states.
items.explain:
Article V requires ratification by three-fourths of the states.

50 × 3/4 = 37.5, and you cannot have half a state, so 38 states are needed.

36 is less than 38, so the amendment is not ratified yet; it needs 2 more states. The most tempting error is using two-thirds (33.3, so 34 states), which is the fraction for proposing an amendment in Congress, not for ratifying it.

items.prompt: The President vetoes a bill, and the House of Representatives, where the bill started, votes on whether to pass it again. All 435 members vote. Based on Document 2, what is the smallest number of "yes" votes needed in the House for the override to move forward to the Senate?

mistakes.why: 218 is a simple majority of 435, which passes an ordinary bill. Document 2 requires "two thirds of that House" to override: 435 × 2/3.
You used three-fourths (435 × 3/4 = 326.25). Three-fourths is the fraction of states needed to ratify an amendment. An override needs two-thirds.

items.hint: Document 2 requires "two thirds of that House." Multiply 435 by 2/3.
items.explain:
Document 2 says the bill moves on "If after such Reconsideration two thirds of that House shall agree to pass the Bill."

435 × 2/3 = 870/3 = 290

The answer is a whole number, so exactly 290 votes reach two-thirds. (If the result had a decimal, you would round up.) A common error is using a simple majority, 218 votes, which is enough to pass an ordinary bill but not to override a veto. After the House, the Senate must also vote by two-thirds.

items.prompt:
Congress passes a law requiring all newspapers to get government approval before printing political articles, and the President signs it. A newspaper challenges the law in court. The Supreme Court rules that the law violates the Constitution and cannot be enforced.

The Supreme Court's action is an example of
options: judicial review, a check by the courts on the other branches
a veto, a check by the courts on the laws passed by Congress
impeachment, a check by Congress on the courts and the judges
federalism, a division of power between the nation and the states
why: Only the President vetoes, and a veto happens before a bill becomes law. This law was already in effect when the Court ruled.
Impeachment is Congress's power to charge and remove officials. Here the Court acted, and it struck down a law, not an official.
Federalism involves the states, and no state government is part of this scenario. The Court is checking Congress and the President.
items.hint: Who acted, and what did they decide about the law?
items.explain:
The Supreme Court (judicial branch) decided that a law made by Congress and signed by the President is unconstitutional. That is judicial review, established in Marbury v. Madison (1803). It checks both the legislative and executive branches.

It is not a veto: only the President vetoes, and a veto happens before a bill becomes law. Impeachment is a power of Congress, not the courts. Federalism is not involved because no state government is part of the scenario.

items.prompt: Read the news summary. Click the sentence that shows the judicial branch checking the executive branch.
spans: In March, the president vetoed a bill that would have raised entrance fees at national parks.
Two weeks later, the House voted 270 to 160 in favor of overriding the veto, short of the two-thirds it needed.
In April, the president nominated a new judge to a federal appeals court.
After hearings, the Senate voted 46 to 54 against confirming the nominee.
In June, a federal court ruled that one of the president's orders on park lands violated the Constitution.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the sentence about nominating a judge. It mentions a court, but there the president is acting on the judicial branch, not the other way around.
items.hint: Find the sentence where a court is the one acting.
items.explain:
Ask who acted and who was limited. In the last sentence, a federal court (judicial) ruled that the president's order (executive) violated the Constitution. That is judicial review used against the executive branch.

The veto is the executive checking Congress. The failed override is Congress trying to check the president (two-thirds of 430 is 286.67, so 287 votes were needed, and 270 is short). The nomination is the executive acting on the courts, and the rejected nominee is the Senate checking the president.

items.prompt:
Complete the statement using Document 4.

The power to coin money is listed in Article I, Section 8, so it is a {{0}} power of the national government. Under the Tenth Amendment, powers that are not given to the national government and not denied to the states are {{1}} to the states or the people. If a valid federal law conflicts with a state law, the {{2}} requires judges to follow the federal law.

options: delegated
reserved
concurrent
denied
why: Reserved powers belong to the states. Coining money is listed for Congress and forbidden to the states.
Concurrent powers are shared, but Article I, Section 10 says no state shall "coin Money," so this power is not shared.
The power is denied to the states, but for the national government it is a power that has been given, or delegated.

options: delegated
reserved
concurrent
prohibited
why: Delegated powers are the ones given to the national government. The Tenth Amendment is about powers not delegated.
Concurrent powers are shared by both levels. The Tenth Amendment keeps leftover powers for the states or the people.
The Tenth Amendment describes powers "not … prohibited" to the states, and says they are "reserved," not prohibited.

options: Supremacy Clause
Necessary and Proper Clause
Commerce Clause
Tenth Amendment
why: The Necessary and Proper Clause lets Congress make laws to carry out its powers. It does not decide conflicts with state law.
The Commerce Clause gives Congress power over trade. It is not the rule that makes federal law win a conflict.
The Tenth Amendment protects state power, so it would not make a federal law win.

items.hint: Delegated = given to the nation. Reserved = kept by the states. Which part says "the supreme Law of the Land"?
items.explain:
Blank 1: delegated. Powers the Constitution lists for Congress, such as coining money, are delegated (also called enumerated) powers. Coining money is not concurrent, because Article I, Section 10 says no state shall "coin Money."

Blank 2: reserved. The Tenth Amendment says those powers "are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people."

Blank 3: Supremacy Clause. Article VI makes the Constitution and federal laws made under it "the supreme Law of the Land," and "the Judges in every State shall be bound thereby." The Tenth Amendment protects state power, so it would not make a federal law win.

items.prompt: Drag each power into the correct category under federalism.
choices: Set up city and county governments
items.why: The most common error is putting "Collect taxes" under national only. Your state and local governments tax too, so the power is shared.
items.hint: Ask: Does only the nation do this, only the states, or both?
items.explain:
• Delegated (national): coining money and making treaties. Article I, Section 10 forbids states to coin money or "enter into any Treaty."
  • Reserved (state): issuing driver's licenses and setting up city and county governments are powers the Constitution leaves to the states.
  • Concurrent (both): the national government and the states both collect taxes and borrow money.

A common error is putting "collect taxes" under national only. Your state and local governments tax too, so it is shared.

items.prompt: According to the graph, how many bills that President Reagan vetoed became law anyway because Congress overrode his veto?
why: 0 is Biden's number of overrides, not Reagan's. Find the "Vetoes overridden" bar above Reagan's name.
69 is 78 − 9, the number of Reagan's vetoes that were not overridden. Those bills did not become law.
78 is Reagan's total number of vetoes. Only the overridden ones became law.
items.hint: When Congress overrides a veto, the bill becomes law. Find Reagan's "Vetoes overridden" bar.
items.explain:
The background text explains that when Congress overrides a veto, "the bill then becomes law." Reagan's "Vetoes overridden" bar shows 9, so 9 vetoed bills became law anyway.

78 is Reagan's total number of vetoes, not the number overridden. 69 (78 − 9) is the number of his vetoes that were not overridden.

items.skill: Point of view in a primary source
items.prompt: Which two statements are supported by Madison's words in Document 3? Select two answers.
options: Government is needed because people are not perfect.
A government must be able to control the people, and it must also be made to control itself.
Regular elections alone are enough to keep a government from abusing its power.
All power should belong to the state governments instead of a national government.
Officials in each branch should set aside their personal interests and never compete with the other branches.
why: Madison calls "a dependence on the people" the primary control, but says experience shows the need for "auxiliary precautions" too. Elections alone are not enough.
Paragraph 2 says power is "divided between two distinct governments," not given entirely to the states.
Madison wants the opposite: officials should have "personal motives to resist encroachments of the others." "Ambition must be made to counteract ambition."
items.hint: Look for the sentences about angels and about "the great difficulty."
items.explain:
Correct: "If men were angels, no government would be necessary" means government exists because people are not perfect. "You must first enable the government to control the governed; and in the next place oblige it to control itself" supports the statement that a government must control the people and also control itself.

Incorrect: Madison calls "a dependence on the people" (elections) the primary control but says experience shows the need for "auxiliary precautions," so elections alone are not enough. Paragraph 2 says power is "divided between two distinct governments," not given entirely to the states. And Madison wants officials to have "personal motives to resist encroachments of the others"; "Ambition must be made to counteract ambition."

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data in the graph?
options: Congress overrode a larger share of George W. Bush's vetoes than of Ronald Reagan's vetoes.
Every president shown in the graph had at least one of his vetoes overridden by Congress.
The more bills a president vetoed, the larger the share of those vetoes Congress overrode.
Presidents after 2000 vetoed fewer bills because they agreed with Congress more often.
why: Check the last pair of bars: Biden had 0 vetoes overridden.
The data contradict this. Reagan vetoed the most bills (78) but had only about 12% overridden, while G. W. Bush vetoed 12 and had about 33% overridden.
The graph shows how many vetoes occurred, not why. Nothing in it shows whether presidents agreed with Congress.
items.hint: Compare shares, not just counts: divide the overrides by the total vetoes for each president.
items.explain:
Compare the share of vetoes overridden:

G. W. Bush: 4 ÷ 12 ≈ 0.33, or about 33%
Reagan: 9 ÷ 78 ≈ 0.115, or about 12%

33% is larger than 12%, so the statement that Congress overrode a larger share of G. W. Bush's vetoes is supported, even though Reagan had more overrides in total.

The statement that every president had at least one override is false: Biden had 0 overrides. The statement that more vetoes mean a larger share overridden is contradicted by the same calculation. The statement about presidents agreeing with Congress gives a reason for the pattern that the graph does not show.

items.prompt: Add up all seven presidents shown in the graph. In all, how many of their vetoes were not overridden by Congress?

mistakes.why: 206 is the total number of vetoes. Subtract the 18 that were overridden: 206 − 18.
18 is the number of vetoes that were overridden. The question asks for the ones that were not: 206 − 18.
69 is Reagan's vetoes that were not overridden (78 − 9). The question asks about all seven presidents combined.

items.hint: Find the total of all vetoes and the total of all overrides, then subtract.
items.explain:
Total vetoes: 78 + 44 + 37 + 12 + 12 + 10 + 13 = 206

Vetoes overridden: 9 + 1 + 2 + 4 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 18

Not overridden: 206 − 18 = 188

A common error is stopping after the first sum (206), which counts all vetoes, including the 18 that Congress overrode.

items.skill: Connecting a source to the Constitution
items.prompt: Which feature of the U.S. Constitution most directly puts into practice Madison's idea in Document 3 that "Ambition must be made to counteract ambition"?
options: The President may veto a bill, and Congress may override the veto by a two-thirds vote of each house.
Members of the House of Representatives must face the voters and run for reelection every two years.
The Preamble lists goals for the new government, such as to "establish Justice" and "secure the Blessings of Liberty."
Article VII required nine of the thirteen states to ratify the Constitution before it could take effect.
why: Frequent elections are a "dependence on the people," which Madison calls the primary control. His ambition line is about branches resisting each other, the "auxiliary precautions."
The Preamble states goals but gives no branch a tool to resist another branch.
Article VII concerns how the Constitution was approved in 1787–1788, not how the branches balance each other.
items.hint: Madison wants each branch to have "constitutional means" to resist the others. Which choice shows two branches pushing against each other?
items.explain:
Madison says each department needs "the necessary constitutional means and personal motives to resist encroachments of the others." The veto and the override give the President and Congress each a tool to resist the other. That is checks and balances, the direct application of "Ambition must be made to counteract ambition."

Frequent House elections are the most tempting wrong answer, but they are a form of "dependence on the people," which Madison calls the primary control, not the branch-against-branch precautions he is describing. The Preamble states goals but gives no branch a tool against another, and Article VII concerns ratification, not the balance among branches.

items.prompt:
A state legislature, facing a budget shortage, passes a law to print its own paper money for use inside the state. The state argues that the Tenth Amendment reserves this power to the states because it affects only people within the state.

Which part of Document 4 most directly shows that the state's argument is wrong?
options: Article I, Section 10, which says no state shall "coin Money; emit Bills of Credit"
Article I, Section 8, which gives Congress the power "To borrow Money on the credit of the United States"
The Tenth Amendment, which says certain powers are reserved "to the States respectively, or to the people"
Article I, Section 8, which gives Congress the power to regulate commerce "among the several States"
why: This clause is about national borrowing, which is a concurrent power. It says nothing about printing money.
This is the clause the state relies on. It cannot show the state's argument is wrong; you need a part that forbids the power.
The state says its money would be used only inside the state, so a clause about trade among states does not answer the argument as directly as an explicit ban.
items.hint: The Tenth Amendment only reserves powers that are not "prohibited by it to the States." Look for a prohibition.
items.explain:
The Tenth Amendment reserves only powers that are neither delegated to the United States "nor prohibited by it to the States." Article I, Section 10 directly prohibits states from coining money or issuing "Bills of Credit" (paper money). Because the Constitution forbids this power to the states, it cannot be reserved to them.

The Tenth Amendment choice is the one the state relies on, so it does not show the argument is wrong. The borrowing clause is about national borrowing, a concurrent power, not printing money. The commerce clause concerns trade among states, but the state says its money would be used only inside the state, so that clause does not answer the argument as directly as the explicit ban.

items.prompt: According to Document 6, what must happen before a treaty the President makes can take effect?
options: Two-thirds of the senators present must agree to it
A majority of the House of Representatives must approve it
The Supreme Court must rule that the treaty is constitutional
The legislature of each state must vote to accept the treaty
why: Document 6 gives the treaty role to the Senate only. The House is not mentioned in the treaty clause.
Document 6 does not mention the courts. Treaty approval belongs to the Senate.
State legislatures appear only in the old rule for choosing senators, not in the treaty clause.
items.hint: Find the word "Treaties" and read the "provided" part that follows.
items.explain:
Article II, Section 2 says the President has power, "by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate, to make Treaties, provided two thirds of the Senators present concur." Concur means "agree." So two-thirds of the senators present must approve. This is a check by the legislative branch on the executive branch.

The most common error is choosing the House, because both houses vote on ordinary laws. Treaties go only to the Senate.

items.prompt: Drag each power into the branch of the national government that holds it.
choices: Veto a bill passed by Congress
Decide what a federal law means in a lawsuit
items.why: The most common mistake is placing "Raise and support an army" with the President. The President commands the army, but Congress creates and pays for it.
items.hint: Congress makes laws and controls money; the President enforces laws and deals with other nations; the courts decide cases.
items.explain:
• Legislative: Congress coins money and raises and supports armies (Article I, Section 8).
  • Executive: the President vetoes bills (Article I, Section 7) and negotiates treaties, which the Senate must approve (Article II, Section 2).
  • Judicial: courts decide what laws mean in actual cases and hear cases involving ambassadors (Article III).

Remember: the President commands the armed forces, but Congress raises and pays for them. That split is itself a check.

items.prompt: According to Document 7, which part of the government has the power to impeach, or formally charge, a federal official?
options: The House of Representatives
The Senate, by a two-thirds vote
The Supreme Court and its justices
The President and the cabinet
why: The Senate has "the sole Power to try all Impeachments." It holds the trial after the House brings the charges.
Document 7 gives the courts no role in impeachment. Congress handles it.
The President can be impeached but has no power to impeach anyone. Document 7 gives that power to the House.
items.hint: Two different houses have two different jobs. Which one has "the sole Power of Impeachment"?
items.explain:
Article I, Section 2 says "The House of Representatives … shall have the sole Power of Impeachment." Sole means "only." The Senate then has "the sole Power to try all Impeachments," and conviction needs two-thirds of the senators present.

The most common error is choosing the Senate. Remember the order: the House charges, the Senate tries.

items.prompt: Two-thirds of the House and two-thirds of the Senate vote to propose an amendment to the Constitution. Under Article V, what must happen next for it to become part of the Constitution?
options: Three-fourths of the states must ratify it
The president must sign it within ten days
The Supreme Court must approve its wording
A majority of voters must approve it nationally
why: This confuses an amendment with an ordinary bill. The president has no role in the amendment process; amendments are not signed or vetoed.
The Supreme Court has no role in approving amendments. Article V sends them to the states.
The Constitution has no national popular vote. Article V gives ratification to the states, through their legislatures or conventions.
items.hint: Article V: propose two-thirds, ratify three-fourths. Who does the ratifying?
items.explain: Article V has two steps: Congress proposes (two-thirds of both houses), and the states ratify (three-fourths, which is 38 of 50). The president does not sign amendments. The most tempting wrong answer treats the amendment like an ordinary bill, which does go to the president.

items.prompt: The House has impeached a federal judge. At the Senate trial, 98 senators are present for the final vote. Based on Document 7, what is the smallest number of senators who must vote to convict for the judge to be removed?

mistakes.why: 98 × 2/3 = 65.33. You rounded down, but 65 is less than two-thirds of 98. Round up to the next whole vote.
67 is two-thirds of a full Senate of 100. Document 7 says two-thirds of the members present, and 98 are present.
50 is a simple majority of 98. Conviction needs "two thirds of the Members present."

items.hint: Multiply the number present by 2/3. If you get a decimal, round up.
items.explain:
Document 7: "no Person shall be convicted without the Concurrence of two thirds of the Members present."

98 × 2/3 = 196/3 = 65.33

65 votes would be less than two-thirds, so round up: 66 votes. A common error is using 67, which applies only when all 100 senators are present.

items.prompt:
The president issues an order closing a federal agency that Congress created by law. Workers at the agency sue. A federal court rules that the president has no constitutional power to close an agency created by Congress, and the agency reopens.

The court's ruling is an example of
options: judicial review, a check by the courts on the executive branch
an override, a check by the courts on the president's veto power
advice and consent, a check by the Senate on the president's choices
the Supremacy Clause, a check by the nation on the power of the states
why: An override is Congress passing a bill over a veto by a two-thirds vote. Courts do not override, and no veto happened here.
Advice and consent is the Senate's power over treaties and appointments. Here a court acted, not the Senate.
The Supremacy Clause settles conflicts between national and state law. No state is involved in this scenario.
items.hint: Who acted, and what did they decide about the president's order?
items.explain: Who acted? A federal court: the judicial branch. Who was limited? The president: the executive branch. The court decided the president's action violated the Constitution. That is judicial review, which applies to actions of the executive as well as laws passed by Congress.

Ask who acted and who was limited. The president (executive) vetoed a bill passed by Congress (legislative). The veto is the executive's main check on Congress.

Passing the bill is Congress doing its normal job. The confirmation is the Senate acting on the president's choice. The lawsuit is about federalism (a state against the nation), and agreeing to hear a case is the courts doing their normal job.

delegated
reserved
implied
why: Delegated powers belong to the nation alone. Because states may also tax, taxing is shared.
Reserved powers belong to the states alone. Because Congress may also tax, taxing is shared.

the approval of the president
a ruling by the Supreme Court
a vote of the state's people

Supremacy
Necessary and Proper
Commerce

items.skill: Point of view in a primary source
items.prompt: Which two statements are supported by the excerpts in Document 8? Select two answers.
options: Putting the power to make, enforce, and judge laws in the same hands is tyranny, even if the people elected those leaders.
The courts must rely on the executive branch to carry out their decisions.
The judiciary is the most powerful branch because it can strike down laws passed by Congress.
Tyranny can occur only when power is held by a single hereditary ruler such as a king.
The legislature controls the military, while the executive controls the nation's money.
why: Hamilton says the opposite: the judiciary has "neither FORCE nor WILL, but merely judgment" and controls neither the sword nor the purse.
Madison says tyranny exists whether power is held by "one, a few, or many" and whether it is "hereditary, self-appointed, or elective."
This reverses Hamilton: the executive "holds the sword" (the military), and the legislature "commands the purse" (money).
items.hint: Read Madison's list of who might hold power, and Hamilton's last sentence about the judiciary.
items.explain:
Correct: Madison says the accumulation of all powers "in the same hands" is tyranny "whether hereditary, self-appointed, or elective," so even elected leaders count. Hamilton says the judiciary "must ultimately depend upon the aid of the executive arm even for the efficacy of its judgments."

Incorrect: Hamilton calls the judiciary the branch with "neither FORCE nor WILL," not the most powerful. Madison's list "one, a few, or many" shows tyranny is not limited to kings. And Hamilton gives the sword to the executive and the purse to the legislature, not the reverse.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the graph and the background text?
options: More than one-third of all amendments were ratified in the period from 1789 to 1800.
Amendments were ratified at a fairly steady rate in each of the periods shown on the graph.
Each period shown on the graph had more amendments ratified than the period before it.
Americans became less interested in changing the Constitution in the years after 2000.
why: The bars swing from 11 to 4 to 12 to 0. That is not a steady rate.
The number fell from 11 to 4 and from 12 to 0, so this is false for two of the changes.
The graph shows that no amendments were ratified after 2000, not why. It says nothing about what Americans were interested in.
items.hint: Find one-third of 27, then compare it to the 1789–1800 bar.
items.explain:
One-third of 27 is 27 ÷ 3 = 9. In 1789–1800, 11 amendments were ratified, and 11 ÷ 27 ≈ 0.41, or about 41%. That is more than one-third, so the conclusion about the 1789–1800 period is supported.

The rate was not steady (11, 4, 12, 0), and the counts did not rise every period. The claim about Americans' interest gives a reason the graph does not show; it shows only how many amendments were ratified.

items.hint: The 1789–1800 bar includes the Bill of Rights. How many amendments in all, and how many are in the Bill of Rights?
items.explain:
Total amendments: 11 + 4 + 12 + 0 = 27 (the text confirms 27).

The Bill of Rights is the first 10.

After the Bill of Rights: 27 − 10 = 17.

A common error is adding only the bars after 1800 (4 + 12 + 0 = 16). That misses the one amendment in the 1789–1800 bar that was not part of the Bill of Rights.

items.skill: Connecting a source to the Constitution
items.prompt: Which feature of the U.S. Constitution most directly puts into practice Madison's warning in Document 8 about "the accumulation of all powers, legislative, executive, and judiciary, in the same hands"?
options: Articles I, II, and III give the power to make, enforce, and interpret laws to three separate branches.
Article I requires every bill to pass both the House of Representatives and the Senate before it goes to the President.
The Tenth Amendment reserves to the states, or to the people, the powers not delegated to the nation.
Article I, Section 2 requires members of the House to be chosen by the people every second year.
why: Requiring two houses divides power within the legislative branch. Madison's warning names three kinds of power: legislative, executive, and judiciary.
The Tenth Amendment divides power between the nation and the states (federalism). Madison's sentence is about legislative, executive, and judicial power.
Elections make leaders answer to the people, but Madison says even "elective" leaders become tyrants if they hold all three powers.
items.hint: Madison names three kinds of power. Which choice separates all three?
items.explain:
Madison warns against putting legislative, executive, and judicial power "in the same hands." The Constitution's direct answer is separation of powers: Article I gives lawmaking to Congress, Article II gives enforcement to the President, and Article III gives judging to the courts.

The two-house Congress is the most tempting wrong answer, because it also divides power. But it divides only the legislative power, and Madison's sentence names all three kinds.

items.prompt:
A coastal state passes a law taxing all cars shipped into its ports from foreign countries. Congress has not approved the tax. The state argues that taxing is a concurrent power, so it may tax whatever it chooses.

Which part of Document 9 most directly shows that the state's argument is wrong?
options: Article I, Section 10, which says no state may tax imports "without the Consent of the Congress"
Article I, Section 8, which gives Congress the power "To lay and collect Taxes, Duties, Imposts and Excises"
The Tenth Amendment, which reserves to the states the powers "not delegated to the United States"
Article IV, Section 1, which requires each state to honor the "public Acts" of every other state
why: This shows Congress may tax, which is why taxing is concurrent. It does not say states are forbidden to tax imports.
The Tenth Amendment supports state power. It cannot show the state is wrong; you need a part that limits the state.
Full Faith and Credit is about states honoring each other's laws and records. It says nothing about taxing foreign goods.
items.hint: A concurrent power can still have limits. Look for the words "No State shall."
items.explain:
Taxing in general is a concurrent power, but the Constitution places specific limits on the states. Article I, Section 10 says "No State shall, without the Consent of the Congress, lay any Imposts or Duties on Imports or Exports." The cars are imports, and Congress has not consented, so the state's tax is not allowed.

Article I, Section 8 is the most tempting wrong answer, but it only shows that Congress may tax. It does not by itself forbid a state from taxing; Section 10 does.

items.prompt: Under the Articles of Confederation, Congress could pass laws but had no national officials to carry them out. Which part of the Constitution most directly fixed this weakness?
options: Article II, which created a president to enforce the laws
Article V, which set out a process for adding amendments
The Great Compromise, which created a Senate with two members per state
The Tenth Amendment, which reserved leftover powers to the states
why: Article V fixed a different weakness: under the Articles, every change needed all 13 states. It does not create anyone to carry out laws.
The Great Compromise settled how states are represented in Congress, the lawmaking branch. It did not create officials to enforce laws.
The Tenth Amendment protects state power. It does not give the national government anyone to enforce its laws.
items.explain: Carrying out, or enforcing, laws is the job of the executive branch. The Articles had no executive. Article II created one: "The executive Power shall be vested in a President." The other choices fixed other problems or dealt with Congress and the states, not enforcement.

items.prompt: The president negotiates a trade treaty with another country. The Senate votes 58 to 42 in favor of the treaty, and the treaty is not approved. Which statement best describes what happened?
options: The legislative branch checked the executive branch, because a treaty needs a two-thirds vote of the Senate
The executive branch checked the legislative branch, because the president can veto a vote of the Senate
The legislative branch checked the executive branch, because a majority of the Senate voted against the treaty
The judicial branch checked the executive branch, because the treaty was found to violate the Constitution
why: This reverses the direction. The Senate acted and the president's treaty was blocked. Presidents cannot veto Senate votes on treaties.
Most senators voted for the treaty (58 to 42). It failed because 58 is short of two-thirds: 100 × 2/3 = 66.67, so 67 votes.
No court was involved. The Senate's vote, not a court ruling, stopped the treaty.
items.explain: A majority (58) voted yes, but a treaty needs two-thirds of the senators present. With 100 voting, that is 67. So the Senate (legislative) blocked the president's treaty (executive). The tempting wrong answer says a majority voted against it, but most senators actually voted in favor.

items.prompt: The phrase "he shall take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed" describes which main job of the president?
options: Enforcing the laws that Congress has passed
Writing new laws and sending them to Congress
Deciding what the laws mean when people disagree
Approving or rejecting the laws that the states pass
why: The excerpt says the president may "recommend" measures, but only Congress makes laws. "Executed" means carried out, not written.
Deciding what laws mean in disputes is the job of the courts (Article III), not the president.
The president has no power to approve or reject state laws. The excerpt is about carrying out the laws of the United States.
items.explain: "Executed" means "carried out." Taking care that the laws are "faithfully executed" means making sure they are enforced. That is the main job of the executive branch. The tempting wrong answer comes from the first sentence: the president may recommend measures, but recommending is not making laws.

Issuing marriage licenses is not denied to the states; it is one of their own powers.

supreme

Delegated powers belong only to the national government, but states also borrow.

items.skill: Point of view in a primary source
items.prompt: Which two statements are supported by Madison's words? Select two answers.
options: The national government would have a limited number of clearly listed powers.
The national government's powers would mostly deal with matters like war, peace, and foreign trade.
The states would lose their power to tax once the Constitution was ratified.
The national government would manage most matters of people's everyday lives and property.
The states should eventually be replaced by a single national government.
why: Madison links taxation mostly to the federal government's work on foreign commerce, but he never says the states would lose the power to tax.
This reverses Madison. He says the states' powers concern "the lives, liberties, and properties of the people."
Madison says state powers are "numerous and indefinite." Nothing in the excerpt suggests replacing the states.
items.explain:
Correct: Madison says federal powers are "few and defined" and will be used "principally on external objects, as war, peace, negotiation, and foreign commerce."

Incorrect: He gives everyday matters ("the lives, liberties, and properties of the people") to the states, not the nation. He never says states lose the power to tax, and he describes state powers as "numerous," not something to be eliminated.

items.prompt: Click the sentence that shows the Supremacy Clause being applied.

items.explain: The Supremacy Clause (Article VI) makes valid federal law "the supreme Law of the Land." It is applied when a state law conflicts with a federal law and the federal law wins, as in the court ruling about the food-label law. The other sentences show local and state powers (taxes, licenses, schools) or Congress using its own power, with no conflict.

vocab.example: The Constitution was signed in Philadelphia on September 17, 1787, and replaced the Articles of Confederation.

vocab.def: The introduction to the Constitution, which states the goals of the government. It does not grant any powers.
vocab.example: The Preamble begins "We the People of the United States."

vocab.def: The idea that the government's power comes from the people.
vocab.example: The words "We the People" express popular sovereignty.

vocab.def: Dividing the government's work among three branches: legislative (makes laws), executive (enforces laws), and judicial (interprets laws).
vocab.example: Congress writes a law, but the president's agencies carry it out.

vocab.def: The system that lets each branch limit the powers of the other two so that no branch becomes too powerful.
vocab.example: The president nominates judges, but the Senate must confirm them.

vocab.def: The president's power to reject a bill passed by Congress.
vocab.example: The president vetoed the bill and sent it back to Congress with a list of objections.

vocab.def: Passing a bill over the president's veto by a two-thirds vote of the members voting in both the House and the Senate.
vocab.example: Congress overrode the veto, so the bill became law without the president's signature.

vocab.def: The House of Representatives formally charging a federal official with wrongdoing. The Senate then holds a trial to decide whether to remove the official.
vocab.example: The House voted to impeach the judge, and the Senate held the trial.

vocab.def: The power of courts to decide whether a law or government action violates the Constitution and to strike it down if it does.
vocab.example: The Supreme Court used judicial review in Marbury v. Madison (1803).

vocab.def: Dividing power between the national government and the state governments.
vocab.example: The national government prints money, while states issue driver's licenses.

vocab.def: Powers the Constitution gives to the national government, mostly listed in Article I, Section 8. Also called enumerated or expressed powers.
vocab.example: Declaring war is a delegated power of Congress.

vocab.def: Powers kept by the states or the people because the Constitution does not give them to the national government or deny them to the states (Tenth Amendment).
vocab.example: Running public schools is a reserved power.

vocab.def: Powers shared by both the national government and the state governments.
vocab.example: Both the national government and the states collect taxes.

vocab.def: The part of Article VI that makes the Constitution, federal laws made under it, and treaties "the supreme Law of the Land." Valid federal law wins over conflicting state law.
vocab.example: Because of the Supremacy Clause, a state cannot enforce a law that conflicts with a valid federal law.

vocab.def: The last clause of Article I, Section 8, which lets Congress make laws needed to carry out its listed powers. Also called the elastic clause.
vocab.example: The Supreme Court relied on it in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) to uphold a national bank.

notes:
Week 2 Study Sheet: The U.S. Constitution

Two ways the Constitution divides power: Separation of powers splits it side to side among three branches. Federalism splits it top to bottom between the nation and the states. Checks and balances let each branch limit the others.

BranchArticleJobChecks it holds
Legislative: Congress (House 435, 2-yr terms; Senate 100, 6-yr terms)IMakes lawsOverride veto (2/3 of each house); approve treaties (Senate, 2/3); confirm appointments (Senate); impeach (House) and remove (Senate, 2/3); control spending; create lower courts
Executive: President (4-yr term, two-term limit)IIEnforces lawsVeto bills; nominate judges and officials; grant pardons
Judicial: Supreme Court and lower courts (judges serve for life)IIIInterprets lawsJudicial review: strike down unconstitutional laws and actions (Marbury v. Madison, 1803)

Structure

  • Articles of Confederation (1781): too weak; no taxes, no president, no national courts
  • Great Compromise: House by population; Senate 2 per state
  • Preamble: "We the People" (popular sovereignty); goals only, no powers
  • Art. IV: states' relations (Full Faith and Credit)
  • Art. V: propose by 2/3 of both houses; ratify by 3/4 of states (38); no role for the president
  • Art. VI: Supremacy Clause, "the supreme Law of the Land"
  • Art. VII: ratification by 9 of 13 states
  • 27 amendments; first 10 = Bill of Rights (1791)

Federalism

  • Delegated (national): coin money, declare war, make treaties, regulate interstate and foreign trade, post offices, armies
  • Reserved (state, 10th Amend.): schools, local governments, driver's and marriage licenses, professional licenses
  • Concurrent (both): tax, borrow, make and enforce laws, set up courts
  • Denied to states (Art. I, Sec. 10): treaties, coining money, taxing imports without Congress's consent
  • Necessary and Proper Clause: implied powers (McCulloch v. Maryland, 1819)

Vote Math

Multiply the members voting by the fraction; if you get a decimal, round up. Two-thirds of 100 = 67; of 99 = 66; of 435 = 290; of 430 = 287. Three-fourths of 50 states = 38. An override must reach two-thirds in each house separately.

Key Quotations Decoded

  • "vested in" = given to; "inferior Courts" = lower courts; "ordain and establish" = create
  • "the very definition of tyranny" (Federalist No. 47) = all powers in the same hands
  • "Ambition must be made to counteract ambition" (Federalist No. 51) = each branch protects its power, checking the others
  • "If men were angels, no government would be necessary" = people and leaders are imperfect, so government must be limited
  • "neither FORCE nor WILL, but merely judgment" (Federalist No. 78) = the courts depend on the other branches

GED tip: On scenarios, ask who acted and who was limited. Two branches = checks and balances; nation and state = federalism. On data, share = part ÷ whole, and a graph shows what happened, not why.
